questions.text: Which architect, the first African laureate, won the Pritzker Prize in 2022?

options.text: David Chipperfield, known for his modernist approach and significant contributions to contemporary architecture
Diébédo Francis Kéré
Alejandro Aravena, recognized for his innovative social housing projects and sustainable design
Wang Shu, celebrated for his integration of traditional Chinese architecture with modern techniques

rationale.correct: Diébédo Francis Kéré won in 2022, becoming the first African Pritzker laureate, honored for community-driven architecture in Burkina Faso.

questions.text: Which year was Frei Otto the Pritzker Prize laureate, becoming the first posthumous award?

rationale.correct: Frei Otto won the Pritzker Prize in 2015 as the first posthumous laureate, honored for his structural and material innovation.

questions.text: A living architect whose built work demonstrates tleant, vision, and lasting contribution to the built environment is recognized annually with a prestigious prize established in 1979. This describes which architecture award?

options.text: American Institute of Architects Gold Medal
Royal Institute of British Architects Medal
Pritzker Architecture Prize
RIBA Stirling Prize

rationale.a: AIA Gold Medal has different criteria.
rationale.b: RIBA Medal has different focus and history.
rationale.d: Stirling Prize recognizes completed buildings, not living architects' lifetime achievement.
rationale.correct: This describes the Pritzker Architecture Prize, established in 1979 by the Hyatt Foundation, recognizing living architects' enduring contributions.

questions.text: In which year was the Pritzker Architecture Prize established?

rationale.a: The prize was not established in 1975.
rationale.c: The prize was established in 1979, not 1985.
rationale.correct: The Pritzker Prize was established in 1979 by the Hyatt Foundation.

questions.text: Who was the first Pritzker Prize laureate in 1979?

options.text: Luis Barragán, known for his colorful and emotional architecture
Philip Johnson
I.M. Pei, celebrated for his modernist architectural designs
Kenzo Tange, a key figure in the Metabolist movement

rationale.a: Luis Barragán won in 1980, the second laureate.
rationale.correct: Philip Johnson was the first Pritzker laureate in 1979, representing American establishment modernism.

questions.text: Which year marked the first femlea Pritzker Prize laureate, breaking a 25-year gender barrier?

rationale.correct: Zaha Hadid became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize in 2004.

questions.text: Which two architects are both first laureates of their respective countries: Wang Shu (China) and which architect (Japan)?

options.text: Kenzo Tange, who received the prize in 1987 for his monumental urban planning works
Tadao Ando, who received the prize in 1995 for his minimalist concrete architecture
Shigeru Ban, who received the prize in 2014 for his innovative humanitarian shelters
Multiple Japanese laureates preceded Wang Shu

rationale.a: Tange won in 1987, predating Wang Shu.
rationale.b: Ando won in 1995, predating Wang Shu.
rationale.c: Ban won in 2014, after Wang Shu.
rationale.correct: Wang Shu was China's first laureate in 2012, but Japan had multiple laureates before him (Tange 1987, Ando 1995, etc.). No Japanese architect was a 'first' along with Wang Shu.

questions.text: In which year did the Pritzker Prize recognize its second Chilean laureate?

rationale.a: Yvonne Farrell & Shelley McNamara won in 2020 (Ireland).
rationale.note: Remove fictional winners; actual 2024 winner: Riken Yamamoto (Japan). No 2025 winner as of March 2026.
rationale.correct: No Pritzker Prize awarded in 2026 as of March 2026; second Chilean laureate has not yet been awarded.

questions.text: Which architect won the Pritzker Prize in 1988, a shared award that was the only shared prize until later team practices?

options.text: Oscar Niemeyer and Gordon Bunshaft
Paul Rudolph and Kevin Roche
James Stirling and Michael Wilford
Aldo Rossi and Carlo Aymonino

rationale.b: Roche won individually in 1982; Rudolph did not win.
rationale.c: Stirling won individually in 1981; Wilford was not a laureate.
rationale.correct: In 1988, Gordon Bunshaft (USA) and Oscar Niemeyer (Brazil) shared the Pritzker Prize—the only shared award until later team practices (SANAA, etc.).

questions.text: Frank Gehry won the Pritzker Prize in 1989. What is his most iconic building, completed in 1997?

options.text: Getty Center, Los Angeles
Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
Dancing House, Prague
Vitra Design Museum, Weil am Rhein

rationale.a: Getty Center is by Richard Meier (1984 laureate, completed 1997).
rationale.c: Dancing House is by Gehry and Vlado Milunić (1999), earlier than Bilbao.
rationale.d: Vitra Design Museum is by Gehry (1989) but predates Bilbao.
rationale.correct: Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (1997) epitomizes his deconstructivist approach with titanium-clad biomorphic forms. He won the Pritzker in 1989, well before this building's completion.

questions.text: Leajandro Aravena won the Pritzker Prize in 2016. For which type of architecture is he primarily recognized?

options.text: Museum design and cultural institutions, focusing on iconic and monumental structures
High-tech commercial architecture, emphasizing cutting-edge technology and innovation
Social housing and community-driven work
Parametric digital design, utilizing advanced computational techniques

rationale.a: Aravena pursues social work, not purely cultural institutions.
rationale.b: Aravena is not known for high-tech commercial work.
rationale.d: Aravena pursues participatory design, not parametricism.
rationale.correct: Alejandro Aravena won in 2016 for social housing and community-driven architecture, exemplified by Quinta Monroy Housing (2004).

questions.text: How do the Pritzker laureate selections from 2010–2024 differ from those in the 1980s in terms of geography, building type, and design philosophy?

options.text: Recent selections are identical to 1980s selections; geography and philosophy have not changed, maintaining a consistent approach
Recent selections increasingly recognize non-Western architects, social impact, and sustainability; 1980s selections emphasized Western formalism and cultural institutions.
Recent selections reject all modernism; 1980s selections embraced modernism exclusively, highlighting a shift in architectural values
Recent selections are less rigorous than 1980s selections; quality has declined, reflecting a perceived drop in standards

rationale.a: Significant philosophical and geographic shifts are evident.
rationale.c: Both eras embrace modernism differently; the distinction is in philosophy and scope.
rationale.d: Recent laureates maintain rigorous standards; the shift is in priorities and representation.
rationale.correct: The article articulates this shift: Early era (1979–1995) rewarded Western modernists and cultural ambition; Recent era (2011–2024) increasingly recognizes Global South architects, social practice, and sustainability (Aravena, Kéré, Ban, Lacaton & Vassal).
